ctx-1968.prompt: Which was the only new study that the National Commission on the Causes and Prevention of Violence funded on its own account?
options: A laboratory experiment measuring children’s behaviour after a violent film
A content analysis of violence in the prime-time programmes of the 1967–68 season
A national fear survey of American adults
An institutional study of the ownership structure of television companies
ctx-1968.explain: The Commission surveyed the existing research and funded a single new study: the 1967–68 season violence content analysis run by Gerbner. The laboratory-experiment option is tempting because we are used to “violence = experiment”; but the starting point of Cultural Indicators was counting the content itself. The national audience survey came later, in the early 1970s.

ctx-bullet.prompt: True or false: Cultivation studies are designed to test whether a person who watches a single violent programme becomes aggressive right afterwards.
ctx-bullet.explain: False. Cultivation studies not the instant effect of a single programme but the cumulative effect of message patterns that repeat over years; the question of short-term imitation belongs to a different research tradition (experiments and social learning). What makes “true” tempting is that when television violence comes up, imitation is the first thing that comes to mind.

people-team.prompt: Who wrote the article “Living with Television: The Violence Profile” (1976)?
options: George Gerbner and Larry Gross
Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw
Paul Hirsch and Michael Hughes
Michael Morgan and W. James Potter
people-team.explain: The 1976 Violence Profile article was written by Gerbner and Gross. McCombs and Shaw are the pair behind agenda-setting; Hirsch and Hughes are the critics who reanalysed the cultivation findings in 1980; Potter criticised the theory conceptually in the 1990s. Memorizing name pairs together with the theory they belong to is the most useful strategy in an exam.

claim-core.prompt: Which of the following best summarizes the central hypothesis of cultivation theory?
options: Viewers choose the programmes they watch to satisfy their needs.
Attitudes change immediately after a programme is watched.
Heavy television viewers perceive the real world as closer to the recurring messages of the television world.
The media determine which issues the public regards as important.
claim-core.explain: The central hypothesis is the relationship between heavy viewing and a perception of reality that fits the television world. The first option is the sentence of the uses and gratifications approach, the second of the hypodermic model, the fourth of agenda-setting; options that mix up theories like this often appear in exams.

claim-storyteller.prompt: According to Gerbner’s three kinds of stories, which group do advertisements belong to?
options: Stories about how things work (fiction)
Stories about how things are (news)
Stories about what to do and what is valuable
Advertisements do not count as stories; they only provide information
claim-storyteller.explain: According to Gerbner, advertisements are “value and choice” stories: they show what is desirable and what to do. Fiction is in the first group (it shows how things work), news in the second. The fourth option contradicts the basic idea of the theory: cultivation treats all media content as part of one story system.

concepts-prongs.prompt: A researcher counts the gender and occupation distribution of the characters in prime-time series. Which prong is this researcher working on?
options: Institutional process analysis
Message system analysis
Cultivation analysis
Selective exposure analysis
concepts-prongs.explain: Counting who appears in the content, how often and in which roles is message system analysis. Institutional process analysis looks at who produces the content and under what pressures; cultivation analysis measures viewers’ beliefs. The third option is tempting because “cultivation” is the name of the theory; but counting content is only one precursor of it.

concepts-viewers.prompt: What kind of questions are participants asked in a cultivation survey?
options: Which programmes they like, and how much
How they interpret television content
Not about television itself, but about their beliefs about safety, trust and values in the real world
What they did after a programme
concepts-viewers.explain: The questions are about the real world; the researcher looks at whether the answers are “TV answers” or answers that fit the real statistics. The options about liking or interpreting programmes are closer to reception and uses-and-gratifications studies; “what they did after a programme” is the question of behavioural experiments.

concepts-mean.prompt: According to Gerbner, what was the main social consequence of heavy television violence?
options: Leading viewers directly to aggressive behaviour
Instilling in viewers the belief that the world is more dangerous and untrustworthy than it really is
Driving people away from television altogether
Increasing trust in news programmes
concepts-mean.explain: The primary claim of cultivation is fear and insecurity: the mean world syndrome. Gerbner said he found the direct contribution to violence negligible. The first option is the most common misunderstanding; the theory is built on perception of the world, not on imitation.

assumptions-myth.prompt: True or false: Cultivation theory assumes that the effect of television reaches the viewer one-way and instantly.
assumptions-myth.explain: False. The theorists regard the effect as slow, cumulative and part of an interaction between message and context; they do not speak of a one-way flow. What makes the wrong answer attractive is that the word “effect” is still identified with the hypodermic model.

how-steps.prompt: Put the steps of a cultivation study in the correct order.
items: The television world is compared with real statistics
A national survey is run with questions that have TV answers
Participants are grouped by how much television they watch
The TV-answer difference is calculated with demographic controls
how-steps.explain: Cultivation begins with content: without knowing what the television world is, it is not clear which answer counts as the “TV answer”. Then come the survey, the grouping and the controlled comparison. Starting with the survey is a common mistake.

how-mainstream.prompt: A heavy television viewer who lives in a high-crime neighbourhood turns out to be markedly more fearful than a light viewer in the same neighbourhood. Which concept best explains this?
options: Mainstreaming
Resonance
Agenda-setting
Selective exposure
how-mainstream.explain: When everyday experience (high crime) and the messages on television overlap, a “double dose” arises; this is called resonance. Mainstreaming, by contrast, is the blurring of differences among different groups in heavy viewers; in the scenario there is no convergence between groups, but an overlap of experience and message.

evidence-profile.prompt: What did Gerbner try to show Congress with the Violence Profile data?
options: That the amount of prime-time violence changed very little from season to season
That television violence was doubling every year
That children became aggressive immediately after watching a violent programme
That there was more violence in news bulletins than in fiction
evidence-profile.explain: According to Britannica, Gerbner used the profiles to show that violence in prime time hardly changed from season to season. The “rising every year” option is tempting because news about violence gives us a feeling of increase; but what the theory is interested in is not change but a stable and lasting message system.

evidence-size.prompt: What is the main finding of Hermann, Morgan and Shanahan’s 2021 meta-analysis?
options: The cultivation effect disappeared completely with cable television.
The overall effect was about .107 and stayed within a narrow range over the decades.
The effect was seen only in very large samples, not in small ones.
Overall viewing showed a weaker effect than genre-specific viewing.
evidence-size.explain: The meta-analysis found an overall effect of .107 and reported that the effect stayed within a narrow range over the decades despite technological change. The fourth option is a reversed answer: the effect of overall viewing came out stronger than that of genre-specific viewing (though it weakened over time). The third option is also reversed: effects were larger in small samples.

critique-hirsch.prompt: Which of the following is the main methodological point of Hirsch’s (1980) critique of cultivation?
options: That survey questions should be asked about television
That the linear relationship disappears when controls are applied simultaneously rather than one at a time
That watching television definitely creates aggression
That the theory can be applied only to news viewers
critique-hirsch.explain: Hirsch’s main argument was that when controls are applied simultaneously, the linear relationship between viewing and the TV answer disappears. The third option is both the opposite and not the theory’s own claim: Hirsch was someone who criticized the theory, not someone who supported it.

critique-causality.prompt: In Doob and Macdonald’s Toronto study, what happened when the neighbourhood’s actual crime rate was taken into account?
options: The relationship between television viewing and fear became even stronger.
The within-neighbourhood relationship became non-significant; no general viewing–fear relationship was seen.
The effect was seen only in children.
The effect among women viewers disappeared.
critique-causality.explain: When all the data from the four neighbourhoods (high and low crime, city centre and suburb) were pooled, the relationship was found; but the average within-neighbourhood relationship was non-significant. The first option is the exact opposite of the criticism: the finding made the theory look weaker and more conditional.

today-digital.prompt: What tendency did Hermann, Morgan and Shanahan’s 2023 social media meta-analysis find?
options: General social media use showed a stronger effect than exposure to specific content.
Exposure to a specific type of content showed a higher effect than general use.
Active use showed a higher effect than passive use.
The effect was seen only in older samples.
today-digital.explain: The meta-analysis reported that in studies of exposure to specific content the effect was higher than for general use; it was also higher in young people, and lower for active use. The third and fourth options state the opposite of the findings.

today-lab.prompt: Of the three prongs of cultivation, which is this mini exercise a simple imitation of?
options: Institutional process analysis
Message system analysis
Cultivation analysis
None of them
today-lab.explain: Sorting the items in a feed into categories and counting them is a simple form of message system analysis. Cultivation analysis is the survey that measures viewers’ beliefs; there is no survey in this exercise. Institutional process analysis looks at who produces the content and under what pressure.

turkey-studies.prompt: How were the survey questions prepared in Özer and Jafarli’s Baku study?
options: The questions were translated word for word from American studies.
A message system analysis of Turkish channels was carried out first; the questions were prepared according to these findings.
The survey was run and no content analysis was done at all.
Only news programmes were examined.
turkey-studies.explain: The study follows the logic of the theory: first a message system analysis (ATV, Kanal D, Star, Show TV), then a survey based on these findings. Starting with the survey (the third option) would break the order of a cultivation study.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question asks: “Which theory argues that heavy television viewing, over the long term, leads people to perceive the real world as similar to the on-screen world?” Which is the correct answer?
options: Agenda-setting
Spiral of silence
Cultivation (in Turkish: ekme / yetiştirme)
The hypodermic (magic bullet) model
exam-patterns.explain: A long-term, cumulative perception of reality is the signature of cultivation. Agenda-setting focuses on which issues are seen as important, the spiral of silence on the fear of being in the minority, the hypodermic model on the instant effect of a single message.

summary.prompt: True or false: According to cultivation, the main effect of television is to lead viewers directly to violence.
summary.explain: False. The focus of cultivation is perception of the world and fear (the mean world syndrome); Gerbner finds the direct contribution to violence negligible.

quiz.prompt: A research team is examining under what commercial and institutional pressures series and news are produced. Which prong of Cultural Indicators is this?
options: Message system analysis
Cultivation analysis
Institutional process analysis
Uses and gratifications analysis
quiz.explain: Asking through which processes and pressures messages are selected and produced is institutional process analysis. Message system analysis counts the content; cultivation analysis measures viewers’ beliefs. The fourth option is the name of a different theory.

quiz.prompt: True or false: According to Gerbner, the main consequence of television violence is that viewers imitate this violence.
quiz.explain: False. Gerbner said he found the direct contribution to violence negligible and put forward as the main consequence the feeling of fear and insecurity (the mean world syndrome). The imitation claim belongs not to cultivation but to the tradition of experiments and social learning.

quiz.prompt: Match the researchers and studies with the contribution they belong to.
pairs: Founder of the Cultural Indicators project; the three-pronged design
Comparison of high-crime and low-crime neighbourhoods in Toronto
Conceptual critique of the theory; three distinct meanings of “cultivation”
A study with 1,280 children in Perth
Meta-analysis of twenty years of studies (average .09)
quiz.explain: Mixing up these pairings is common in exams. Gerbner is the founder; Doob and Macdonald are critics who took the actual crime rate into account; Potter is the conceptual critic; Hawkins and Pingree replicated the finding with children in Australia; the Morgan–Shanahan meta-analysis is a survey of the evidence by the theory’s own defenders.

quiz.prompt: Put the events in chronological order (oldest to newest).
items: The Commission funds the 1967–68 season violence content analysis (1968)
The Surgeon General’s committee and 23 projects (1969)
Gerbner and Gross’s Violence Profile article (1976)
quiz.explain: The order is: 1968 commission, 1969 committee, 1976 Violence Profile, 1980 mainstreaming, 1993 Potter, 2023 social media meta-analysis. Mixing up the Violence Profile and the mainstreaming article is a frequent mistake: the first contains the first results, the second is a response to the first criticisms.

quiz.text: The tendency of heavy viewers to have the differences of opinion between different groups eroded and to move closer to a common view is called {{1}}; the overlap of everyday experience and television messages that increases the effect is called {{2}}.

options: mainstreaming
agenda-setting
selective perception
priming
resonance
spiral of silence
framing
gatekeeping

quiz.explain: Mainstreaming is the convergence that erodes differences; resonance is experience and message overlapping to create a “double dose”. The other options belong to other theories: agenda-setting, priming, framing and the spiral of silence are the topics of separate lessons of ours.

quiz.scenario: A student runs a survey of 200 people on campus: “Would you be afraid to walk alone on campus at night?” and daily television viewing time. Heavy viewers are more afraid. The student wants to present the result as “television frightens people”. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: Which prong of Cultural Indicators does this study correspond to, and what is missing?
options: Cultivation analysis; but there is no content analysis of the television world
Message system analysis; but there is no survey
Institutional process analysis; but the sample is small
None of them, because cultivation does not use surveys
parts.explain: The survey and the grouping are cultivation analysis. But there is no content analysis (message system) that would define the “TV answer”. The fourth option is wrong: cultivation analysis is done precisely with a survey.

parts.prompt: What would a Doob-and-Macdonald-style objection be?
options: The actual level of crime or danger on campus may affect both viewing and fear.
Students don’t watch television anyway.
Survey questions should be asked about television.
The effect is seen only in children.
parts.explain: The Toronto study showed that the relationship disappeared when the actual crime rate of the neighbourhood was controlled. In the student’s study too, a third factor (the actual level of safety) could explain the relationship.

parts.prompt: Which concept is the cultivation side’s answer to this objection?
options: Resonance: the overlap of experience and message increases the effect
Agenda-setting
Priming
Spiral of silence
parts.explain: The Gerbner team argued that everyday experience and television messages together create a “double dose”. The other options are concepts of other theories.

quiz.takeaway: A cultivation study needs both content and a survey; and real-world conditions (crime rate, neighbourhood) must always be controlled for as a third factor.

quiz.prompt: What conclusion did Hermann, Morgan and Shanahan’s (2021) meta-analysis reach?
options: The effect disappeared over the decades.
The overall effect was about .107 and stayed within a narrow range over the decades.
The effect was seen only among news viewers.
The effect is large and growing.
quiz.explain: The meta-analysis found an overall effect of .107 from 3,842 effect sizes and reported that the effect stayed within a narrow range over the decades. “Disappeared” and “growing” are two opposite caricatures of the finding.

quiz.prompt: True or false: Hirsch (1980), by reanalysing the Gerbner team’s data, argued that the cultivation hypothesis lacks empirical support.
quiz.explain: True. Hirsch argued that when controls are applied simultaneously, no linear relationship remains between viewing and the TV answer, and that the hypothesis has no empirical support. The Gerbner team, for its part, replied.

quiz.prompt: What did Williams’s (2006) one-month online game experiment find?
options: Players’ fear of all real-world crimes increased.
Players’ perception of danger changed only for the dangers seen in the game world.
The game had no effect on perception.
The effect was seen only in child players.
quiz.explain: The change in perception was limited to the events and situations encountered in the game; this did not fit the broader spread predicted by some cultivation researchers. The first option is precisely the claim of this broader spread, and is not the finding.

quiz.prompt: “Heavy television viewers see the world as more dangerous and insecure than it really is.” Which concept does this statement sum up?
options: Mainstreaming
The mean world syndrome
The spiral of silence
Priming
quiz.explain: This is Gerbner’s definition of the mean world syndrome. Mainstreaming describes convergence among different groups, the spiral of silence describes staying silent out of fear of being in the minority, and priming describes a news frame influencing evaluations.

quiz.scenario: A youth researcher is reading the 2023 social media meta-analysis and wants to design a study that measures “what kind of content” young people are exposed to rather than “how much time” they spend. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: Which meta-analysis finding is this choice consistent with?
options: Exposure to specific content showed a higher effect than general use.
General use showed a higher effect than specific content.
Active use showed the highest effect.
There was an effect only in European samples.
parts.explain: In the 2023 meta-analysis the effect in studies of exposure to specific content was higher than for general use. The second and third options are reversed findings; the fourth names the wrong region (the higher effect was in Asian samples).

parts.prompt: How should the researcher interpret young people’s personalized feeds?
options: Because everyone sees the same feed, the message system is shared.
In personalized feeds the assumption of a shared message system is called into question; this is our interpretation, not a documented finding.
Cultivation can be applied only to television.
Feeds create a mean world; the evidence is certain.
parts.explain: Personalized feeds strain the shared-message-system assumption; but this is an interpretation and needs evidence. The “certain” option goes beyond the limits of the evidence; the “only television” option ignores the existence of social media studies.

quiz.takeaway: To test cultivation in digital settings, the question “what kind of content” rather than “how much” may be more productive; but the assumption of a shared message system needs to be tested in this environment.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following correctly states the difference between cultivation and agenda-setting?
options: Cultivation studies which issues are seen as important, while agenda-setting studies long-term perception of reality.
Cultivation studies long-term perception of social reality, while agenda-setting studies which issues are seen as important.
Both study the instant effect of a single message.
Both concern only news content.
quiz.explain: Cultivation looks at long-term perception of reality (especially the total story system of television); agenda-setting looks at which issues the media foreground and how this affects perceived importance in public opinion. The first option gives the two swapped; this kind of reversal trap is the most frequent one in exams.
